10	## 1. Conventions and a direct-limit observation

12	Write \(D=T\), \(D_n=T_n\), and
13	\[
14	P_m=(1-t_1)\cdots(1-t_m).

18	Under these identifications,

21	\]
22	Indeed, every right \(D\)-linear map \(D\to D\) has the form \(x\mapsto ax\). In particular, \(d_0=1\).

24	We will use the following elementary observation.
25	
26	### Direct-limit duality lemma
27	Suppose a \(D\)-\(D\)-bimodule \(V\) is an increasing union of bimodules
28	\[
29	V_n\cong D_n^2,
30	\]
31	where the displayed bases are centralizing bases: left and right multiplication by \(D_n\) agree on each basis vector. Use a cofinal sequence of indices, and suppose the coordinate transition from \(V_n\) to the next stage is
32	\[
33	x\longmapsto B_nx
34	\]
35	for column coordinates, with \(B_n\) invertible over the next division ring.
36	
37	Then:
38	
39	1. \(V_D\) has dimension \(2\).
40	2. Its right dual \(V^*=\operatorname{Hom}_D(V,D)\) is again a union of standard two-dimensional local bimodules.
41	3. The coordinate transition matrices for \(V^*\) are
42	   \[
43	   J(B_n):=(B_n^{-1})^{\mathsf T}.
44	   \]
45	
46	**Proof.** Invertibility means that a basis at any stage remains a right basis at every later stage. Its two vectors therefore form a right \(D\)-basis of the union.
47	
48	A functional with row coordinates \(r\) must have row coordinates
49	\[
50	r'=rB_n^{-1}
51	\]
52	at the next stage, because \(r'x'=rx\). In column coordinates this is the transition \(J(B_n)\).
53	
54	These local duals exhaust the global dual. To see this, fix a basis at the first stage. The two values of a global functional belong to some \(D_m\); after enlarging \(m\), its values on the stage-\(m\) basis belong to \(D_m\) as well. Conversely, a local functional extends uniquely using the invertible transition matrices. The bimodule actions agree with these extensions. ∎
55	
56	Thus, to compute all the \(d_j\), it will suffice to find local transition matrices for \(N_1\) and prove that every forward iterate of \(J\) is invertible.
57	
58	## 2. Two-dimensional local models for \(N_1\)
59	
60	The quantum Laurent monomials have the usual normal form
61	\[
62	t^a=t_1^{a_1}\cdots t_m^{a_m},\qquad a\in\mathbb Z^m,
63	\]
64	and multiplication is
65	\[
66	t^at^b
67	=
68	2^{-\sum_{i=1}^{m-1}a_{i+1}b_i}\,t^{a+b}.
69	\tag{1}
70	\]
71	For example, this follows directly by constructing the algebra as an iterated skew Laurent extension. Consequently the monomials are linearly independent. We will use, in particular, the resulting transcendence of a new skew Laurent variable over the preceding division ring.
72	
73	Take even \(n\ge2\), and put
74	\[
75	z_n=t_1t_3\cdots t_{n-1},\qquad
76	c_n=z_nt_{n+1}.
77	\]
78	The relations give
79	\[
80	c_n\in Z(D_{n+1}),\qquad z_nt_n=2t_nz_n.
81	\tag{2}
82	\]
83	Moreover, \(c_n\) is transcendental over \(D_n\), and
84	\[
85	t_{n+1}=z_n^{-1}c_n.
86	\]
87	
88	Inside \(N_1={}_DD_\kappa\), define
89	\[
90	V_n=D_n\kappa(D_n),
91	\]
92	where this notation means the additive span of the products. These bimodules form an increasing union equal to \(D\), since \(V_n\) contains \(D_n\).
93	
94	For \(a\in D_n\),
95	\[
96	\kappa(a)=P_{n+1}aP_{n+1}^{-1}.
97	\]
98	It follows that
99	\[
100	\theta_n:V_n\longrightarrow D_{n+1},\qquad
101	\theta_n(x)=xP_{n+1},
102	\]
103	is a bimodule map when the right copy of \(D_n\) is identified through \(\kappa\). Its image is
104	\[
105	D_nP_{n+1}D_n
106	=D_n(1-t_{n+1})D_n
107	=D_n\oplus D_nc_n.
108	\tag{3}
109	\]
110	
111	Here is justification of the last equality. The left side is contained in the right side because \(c_n\) centralizes \(D_n\). Also,
112	\[
113	(1-z_n^{-1}c_n)a-a(1-z_n^{-1}c_n)
114	=(az_n^{-1}-z_n^{-1}a)c_n.
115	\]
116	By (2), some \(a\in D_n\) makes the coefficient nonzero. Thus the bimodule contains \(c_n\), and then it contains \(1\). The sum is direct by transcendence.
117	
118	We therefore have a centralizing basis
119	\[
120	e_{n,0}=P_{n+1}^{-1},\qquad
121	e_{n,1}=c_nP_{n+1}^{-1}
122	\tag{4}
123	\]
124	of \(V_n\).
125	
126	### The transition matrix
127	
128	Set
129	\[
130	c=c_n,\qquad s=t_{n+2},\qquad c'=c_{n+2}=ct_{n+3}.
131	\]
132	Both \(c\) and \(s\) centralize \(D_n\), and
133	\[
134	cs=2sc.
135	\tag{5}
136	\]
137	Since
138	\[
139	P_{n+3}=P_{n+1}(1-s)(1-t_{n+3}),
140	\]
141	the images under \(\theta_{n+2}\) of the two old basis vectors are
142	\[
143	(1-s)(1-c^{-1}c'),\qquad
144	c(1-s)(1-c^{-1}c').
145	\]
146	Thus the column-coordinate transition matrix is
147	\[
148	A(c,s)=
149	\begin{pmatrix}
150	1-s&c(1-s)\\
151	-(1-s)c^{-1}&-c(1-s)c^{-1}
152	\end{pmatrix}.
153	\tag{6}
154	\]
155	
156	Notice that its transpose factors as
157	\[
158	A(c,s)^{\mathsf T}
159	=
160	\begin{pmatrix}1\\c\end{pmatrix}
161	\begin{pmatrix}1-s&-(1-s)c^{-1}\end{pmatrix}.
162	\]
163	The transpose is singular. Nevertheless, \(A\), and every forward inverse-transpose iterate of \(A\), is invertible. That asymmetry is the essential calculation.

165	## 3. All forward inverse-transpose iterates are invertible
166	
167	Work in the division ring generated by \(c,s\) with \(cs=2sc\).
168	
169	For a matrix \(F(s)\) over the commutative field \(\mathbb Q(s)\), define
170	\[
171	R_r(F)=
172	\begin{pmatrix}c^r&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}
173	F(s)
174	\begin{pmatrix}c^{-r}&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix},
175	\qquad r\in\{1,-1\}.
176	\]
177	If \(I(s)=F(s)^{-1}\), direct entrywise calculation using
178	\(cf(s)=f(2s)c\) gives
179	\[
180	J(R_r(F))=R_{-r}(\Phi_r(F)),
181	\tag{7}
182	\]
183	where
184	\[
185	\Phi_r(F)=
186	\begin{pmatrix}
187	I_{11}(2^{2r}s)&I_{21}(2^rs)\\
188	I_{12}(2^rs)&I_{22}(s)
189	\end{pmatrix}.
190	\tag{8}
191	\]
192	No rule interchanging transpose and multiplication in a noncommutative ring is being assumed here.
193	
194	For a central parameter \(v\), put
195	\[
196	E_v(s)=
197	\begin{pmatrix}
198	1-\frac{v^2s}{2}&v(1-s)\\
199	-v(1-s)&2s-v^2
200	\end{pmatrix}
201	\]
202	and
203	\[
204	O_v(s)=\frac1s
205	\begin{pmatrix}
206	2s-\frac{v^2}{4}&\frac v2(1-2s)\\
207	-\frac v2(1-2s)&1-\frac{v^2s}{2}
208	\end{pmatrix}.
209	\]
210	Define
211	\[
212	\delta(v)=\frac{(2-v^2)^2}{2},\qquad
213	\epsilon(v)=\frac{(4-v^2)^2}{8}.
214	\]
215	Their ordinary commutative determinants are
216	\[
217	\det E_v=\delta(v)s,\qquad
218	\det O_v=\frac{\epsilon(v)}s.
219	\tag{9}
220	\]
221	Furthermore,
222	\[
223	\Phi_1(E_v)=\delta(v)^{-1}O_v,\qquad
224	\Phi_{-1}(O_v)=\epsilon(v)^{-1}E_{v/2}.
225	\tag{10}
226	\]
227	These are identities of rational-function matrices in \(s,v\).
228	
229	The matrix in (6) is
230	\[
231	A(c,s)=R_1(E_1).
232	\tag{11}
233	\]
234	Equations (7)–(10) show inductively that
235	\[
236	J^{2k}(A)=R_1(\lambda_k E_{2^{-k}})
237	\tag{12}
238	\]
239	for nonzero rational numbers \(\lambda_k\), and that the intervening odd iterates are nonzero rational scalar multiples of
240	\[
241	R_{-1}(O_{2^{-k}}).
242	\]
243	Indeed, one can take
244	\[
245	\lambda_0=1,\qquad
246	\lambda_{k+1}
247	=\lambda_k\frac{\delta(2^{-k})}{\epsilon(2^{-k})}.
248	\]

250	\[
251	0<2^{-2k}\le1,
252	\]
253	so neither \(\delta(2^{-k})\) nor \(\epsilon(2^{-k})\) vanishes. By (9), every matrix in (12), and every intervening odd iterate, is invertible.

256	\[
257	A,\ J(A),\ J^2(A),\ldots.
258	\]
259	All are invertible. Consequently,
260	\[
261	\boxed{d_j=2\quad\text{for every }j\ge1.}
262	\tag{13}
263	\]
264	
265	## 4. Why the left dimension must be infinite
266	
267	We give an algebraic argument that extracts this conclusion from the entire dual-dimension sequence. This also avoids relying on an unproved claim about left independence in the quantum division rings.
268	
269	### Reflection lemma
270	Let \(X\) be an \(E\)-\(F\)-bimodule with finite right dimension \(d\), and let
271	\[
272	X^*=\operatorname{Hom}_F(X,F).
273	\]
274	Consider representations
275	\[
276	\alpha:V\longrightarrow X\otimes_F W,
277	\]
278	where \(V\) is a finite-dimensional left \(E\)-space and \(W\) is a finite-dimensional left \(F\)-space.
279	
280	There is a natural adjunction
281	\[
282	\operatorname{Hom}_E(V,X\otimes_F W)
283	\cong
284	\operatorname{Hom}_F(X^*\otimes_E V,W).
285	\tag{14}
286	\]
287	If \(\beta:X^*\otimes_E V\to W\) corresponds to \(\alpha\), taking its kernel gives the reflection
288	\[
289	\ker\beta\ \longrightarrow X^*\otimes_E V.
290	\]
291	
292	This is an equivalence between:
293	
294	- representations for which \(\beta\) is surjective; and
295	- representations for \(X^*\) whose displayed arrow is injective.
296	
297	Its inverse takes the cokernel and uses (14). It preserves indecomposability.
298	
299	If an injective representation for \(X^*\) has dimension pair \((a,b)\), its inverse reflection has dimension pair
300	\[
301	(b,db-a).
302	\tag{15}
303	\]
304	
305	For completeness, the dimension formula follows because \(X^*\) has left \(F\)-dimension \(d\). The equivalence follows from the mutually inverse kernel/cokernel constructions. Finally, an indecomposable representation with both vertex spaces nonzero has injective displayed arrow: a nonzero kernel would split off a source-simple summand. 306	
307	Now apply this lemma to the successive bimodules \(N_j\), with their original alternating division rings.
308	
309	Fix any integer \(r\ge1\). At level \(r\), start with the sink-simple representation, of dimension pair
310	\[
311	(0,1).
312	\]
313	Inverse-reflect down to level \(0\). At levels \(r-1,\ldots,1\), the dimension rule is
314	\[
315	(a,b)\longmapsto(b,2b-a),
316	\]
317	by (13). It produces
318	\[
319	(0,1),\ (1,2),\ (2,3),\ldots,
320	\]

322	\[
323	(r-1,r)\longmapsto(r,1).
324	\]
325	Every representation constructed remains indecomposable. After the first reflection both dimensions are positive, so its displayed arrow is injective and the next inverse reflection is permitted.
326	
327	At level \(0\) we therefore obtain an injective left \(H\)-linear map
328	\[
329	H^r\longrightarrow N_0\otimes_T T\cong T.
330	\]
331	Hence
332	\[
333	\dim({}_HT)\ge r.
334	\]
335	Since \(r\) was arbitrary,
336	\[
337	\boxed{\ell=\infty.}
338	\tag{16}
339	\]
